newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine president removes premier by decree.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine president removes premier by decree.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma, under pressure from Western donors to sack Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, removed him by decree on Thursday but Kuchma's press office said it was because he was unwell.
His office quoted the decree as saying First Deputy Prime Minister Vasyl Durdynets had been appointed acting prime minister "for the time of Pavlo Lazarenko's illness".
But Lazarenko's aides said he was fine and that the decree effectively meant that the fifth Ukrainian prime minister since Kiev broke free of Soviet rule in 1991 had been sacked.
Rumours have swirled for months in Kiev of Lazarenko's impending dismissal, but until Thursday he had survived a lengthy cabinet reshuffle Kuchma said would help reforms.
Diplomatic and business sources say Kuchma has faced repeated demands for Lazarenko's head from Western officials who see him as an anti-reformist force.
"There has been tremendous pressure for weeks from fairly influential sources to sack Lazarenko," one analyst said.
Ukraine, only briefly independent in history, is third in line after Israel and Egypt for aid from Washington which has a strategic interest in prolonging its freedom from Moscow rule.

During a visit to Canada to drum up business this month, Lazarenko faced a critical front-page article in an influential Toronto newspaper which cited Western intelligence reports carried by the New York Times.
They estimated Lazarenko gained about $260 million from unofficial involvement in United Energy Systems, which had a licence to import cheap Russian gas -- a charge he denies.

Lazarenko, who declared an official income of only a few thousand dollars last year, said during his trip that he was trying to root out corruption in his state of 51 million -- but stressed he was not personally involved.
Lazarenko failed to appear at Thursday's evening session of parliament, when deputies were considering this year's long-delayed budget. Speaker Olexander Moroz said he was ill.

The head of parliament's anti-corruption committee said earlier he had documents showing Lazarenko's office lent almost $11 million for 10 years at an annual five percent interest rate to a firm in Dnipropetrovsk where he was once a regional leader.
It was not clear if Kuchma, who has repeatedly criticised Lazarenko and the government for failing to pass reforms, could re-appoint Lazarenko at a later stage.

But Lazarenko's aides said the reference to ill-health was a ploy, noting that he was in well enough to meet Kuchma earlier in the day and had been in good form when he held talks with leaders of striking coal miners on Wednesday.
One reformist deputy, Serhiy Teryokhin, was quoted by Interfax-Ukraine news agency as noting Kuchma had the right to appoint an acting prime minister for 45 days due to illness.
Teryokhin suggested Lazarenko could resign after that, although Lazarenko said on Wednesday his resignation would not help the country.
Another deputy, Olexander Lavrynovych, told the agency he saw no need for the decree as the prime minister's first deputy should fill his post automatically if he was ill.
Durdynets, a former police general considered to be politically weak, has never been earmarked by analysts as a replacement if rumours of Lazarenko's dismissal proved true.
One replacement could be Anatoly Kinakh, president of the influential Ukrainian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs -- the body which Kuchma led when he ran for president in 1994.
Kinakh recently said he had joined an unaligned group of deputies in parliament to lobby for laws to be passed to overcome Ukraine's economic crisis.
Lazarenko's predecessor Yevhen Marchuk was sacked in May 1996 and accused of mishandling the economy and promoting his own political image.
